summary: Describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange protocol, a component of IPsec used to authenticate both sides and to set up and maintain security associations. It replaced RFC 4306 and folded in the clarifications from RFC 4718. It was itself replaced by RFC 7296.

eli5.summary: Before two computers can talk secretly with IPsec, they have to prove who they are and agree on secret keys. IKEv2 is the handshake that does this. A newer document has replaced this one.

questions: how does ipsec key exchange work
subtitle: How two IPsec peers prove who they are, agree on algorithms and keys, and keep those keys fresh.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs shared state between sender and receiver (algorithms, keys and services), and setting it up by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: IKE performs mutual authentication and sets up an IKE security association with a Diffie-Hellman exchange in four messages, then creates, rekeys and deletes Child SAs for ESP or AH through further request/response exchanges.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5996 clarified and replaced RFC 4306 and RFC 4718 with minimal changes. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 7296.

today: RFC 5996 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7296. It was updated by RFC 5998 and RFC 6989, and it replaced RFC 4306 and RFC 4718.

sections.title: What IKE Does and Where It Is Used
sections.content:
IPsec provides confidentiality, data integrity, access control and data source authentication to IP datagrams by maintaining shared state between the source and the sink. Setting that state up manually does not scale, so the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) does it dynamically. IKE performs mutual authentication between two parties and builds an IKE security association (SA). From that, it can efficiently create SAs for ESP or AH, which the RFC calls Child SAs. It can also negotiate IP compression.

The RFC walks through usage scenarios: gateway to gateway in tunnel mode, endpoint to endpoint in transport mode, and a roaming endpoint connecting to a security gateway in tunnel mode. In the last case IKEv2 offers configuration payloads so the initiator can ask for an IP address owned by the gateway.

RFC 5996 is not a new protocol. IKEv2 was a non-backward-compatible change from version 1 (RFCs 2407, 2408 and 2409), but this document replaces RFC 4306 and RFC 4718 and makes minimum changes to the protocol. It keeps major version 2 and minor version 0.
sections.eli5: Two friends want to pass notes in a secret code. Doing the code setup by hand each time would be a pain, so IKE is a quick routine that sets it up automatically.

sections.title: The Four-Message Initial Exchange
sections.content:
All IKE traffic comes in request/response pairs, and the requester is responsible for retransmitting if no answer arrives. Communication always starts with two exchanges, IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH, normally four messages in total.

In IKE_SA_INIT the initiator sends its proposed algorithms (SAi1), its Diffie-Hellman value (KEi) and a nonce (Ni). The responder picks a suite, completes the Diffie-Hellman exchange and sends its own nonce. Both sides can now derive SKEYSEED and from it the keys SK_e (encryption), SK_a (integrity) and SK_d (for Child SA keys), with separate keys per direction.

In IKE_AUTH, which is encrypted and integrity protected, each side sends its identity, an AUTH payload proving knowledge of the secret behind that identity, and the first Child SA proposal with traffic selectors. Both sides MUST verify that all signatures and MACs are correct. If the Child SA cannot be created, the IKE SA is still established. If the initiator guessed the wrong Diffie-Hellman group, the responder answers with INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD and the initiator MUST retry with the corrected group and propose its full set of suites again, because the rejection was unauthenticated.

Later exchanges are CREATE_CHILD_SA, which makes a Child SA, and INFORMATIONAL, which deletes an SA, reports errors or does housekeeping. An informational request with no payloads is commonly used as a liveness check.
sections.eli5: First they agree on a secret handshake and swap random numbers. Then, using that secret, they show their IDs. After that, they can set up as many secret tunnels as they like.

sections.title: The IKE Header and Payloads
sections.content:
IKE uses UDP ports 500 and 4500, one message per datagram. On port 4500 four octets of zero are prepended and are not counted in IKE's length fields. Every message starts with the IKE header, followed by payloads chained by a Next Payload field. An Encrypted payload MUST be the last payload in a packet, and it MUST NOT contain another Encrypted payload.

The header holds the two 8-octet SPIs (connection identifiers), the next payload type, major and minor version (4 bits each), an exchange type, flags, a 4-octet Message ID and a 4-octet length. Implementations of this version MUST set the major version to 2 and the minor to 0. The exchange types are 34 for IKE_SA_INIT, 35 for IKE_AUTH, 36 for CREATE_CHILD_SA and 37 for INFORMATIONAL.

The flags include R (this is a response), I (sent by the original initiator) and V (the sender can speak a higher major version). The Message ID matches requests with responses, identifies retransmissions, and is essential to the protocol's replay protection.

The Initiator's SPI MUST NOT be zero. The Responder's SPI MUST be zero in the first message of an initial exchange, including repeats that include a cookie.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a label showing which conversation it belongs to, what kind of message it is, and which number in the conversation it is.

sections.title: Cookies, Rekeying and NAT Traversal
sections.content:
Two expected attacks on IKE are state and CPU exhaustion by floods of requests from forged addresses. When a responder sees a large number of half-open IKE SAs, it SHOULD answer IKE_SA_INIT with a COOKIE notification of 1 to 64 octets. The initiator MUST then retry with the cookie as the first payload. The RFC suggests a stateless way to build it from a secret, the initiator's nonce, IP address and SPI, but the exact method does not affect interoperability.

Keys should be used only for a limited time, so SAs are rekeyed: a new equivalent SA is created and the old one deleted, ideally before the old one expires. Unlike IKEv1, lifetimes are not negotiated; each end enforces its own policy. Rekeying an IKE SA uses CREATE_CHILD_SA, the new IKE SA inherits the Child SAs, and the Delete payload for the old IKE SA MUST be the last request sent over it.

Because NATs rewrite addresses and ports, IKEv2 uses UDP encapsulation of IKE and ESP packets. IKE packets MUST be sent to and from port 500 or 4500 but MUST be accepted from any port, and responses go back to the port they came from.

IKE implementations MUST handle messages up to 1280 octets and SHOULD handle up to 3000 octets. IKE has no fragmentation of its own, so the RFC suggests using Hash and URL certificate encodings to keep messages small.
sections.eli5: If a stranger floods the front desk with fake visitors, the desk first sends back a ticket and only helps people who come back with it. Secret codes also get swapped for new ones from time to time, like changing a password.

sections.title: Conformance and Differences from RFC 4306
sections.content:
A minimal IKEv2 implementation may leave out NAT traversal, temporary IP addresses, EAP authentication, window sizes above one, multiple SAs per IKE SA and rekeying. Every implementation MUST be able to do the four-message initial exchange creating one IKE SA and one ESP or AH SA, parse every payload type, and respond to an INFORMATIONAL exchange. To be called conforming, it MUST be configurable to accept PKIX certificates with RSA keys of size 1024 or 2048 bits, and shared key authentication.

Changes from RFC 4306 include clarified SHOULD and MUST language, removal of the discussion of nesting AH and ESP, removal of the INTERNAL_ADDRESS_EXPIRY attribute, a rule that implementations MUST NOT reject messages for payload order, a requirement that the KEi payload MUST be included when rekeying an IKE SA, and new sections on error handling, simultaneous rekeying, NAT traversal in transport mode and exchange collisions. The RFC says the small number of technical changes are not expected to affect deployed RFC 4306 implementations.
sections.eli5: A simple version only has to do the basics, and fancy extras are optional. This new edition mostly cleans up the instructions without changing how the handshake works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The initiator must identify itself first, and usually authenticates first, so that responders are not easily probed. With EAP the order changes and the responder proves its identity first. Because IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH happen before the initiator is authenticated, implementations must be robust against denial-of-service attacks from unauthenticated peers.

Repeated rekeying through CREATE_CHILD_SA without fresh Diffie-Hellman exchanges leaves all SAs open to cryptanalysis of a single key, so implementers should limit that. A PRF whose output is below 128 bits MUST NOT be used, and implementations MUST NOT negotiate NONE as the IKE integrity algorithm or ENCR_NULL as the IKE encryption algorithm. Pre-shared keys should carry as much randomness as the strongest negotiated key, and deriving one from a password is not secure.

Non-key-generating EAP methods SHOULD be avoided, and an implementation using EAP MUST authenticate the server to the client with public keys first. The NAT detection hashes do not reliably hide internal addresses, so designers should not assume IKE will not leak them.
sections.eli5: Use strong random secrets, do not use easy-to-guess passwords as the key, and change keys with a fresh handshake every so often so one stolen key does not unlock everything.

messages.note: IKE_AUTH response completes the IKE SA and first Child SA.

fields.name: IKE SA Initiator's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the initiator; MUST NOT be zero.

fields.name: IKE SA Responder's SPI
fields.desc: Chosen by the responder; zero in the first message of an initial exchange.

fields.desc: Type of the payload that follows the header.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Matches requests to responses and guards against replay.

fields.desc: Total message length, header plus payloads, in octets.
